problems.description: 21 convention violations per static analysis (score 0.81): module-level constants in store.py, transport.py, and multiple __init__.py files are not UPPER_CASE, and naming rules (snake_case functions / PascalCase classes) are missed in __init__.py modules.
app.py contains a class that does not follow the PascalCase pattern required by conventions/python.yaml.

Visible module layout (messages/registry/server) is clean, but the full 18-file commit adds app.py, store.py, and transport.py whose exact roles are not visible in the truncated diff — worth confirming they map to the story's forward sessions (Redis pub/sub, persistence) rather than dead scaffolding.

strengths: Session-1 spec compliance is exact: websockets library (not Flask-SocketIO), asyncio, unique per-client IDs, broadcast, clean disconnect handling, and GET /health returning connected client count.
Wire contract matches the story prompt precisely: {type: str, payload: dict, timestamp: str} with only broadcast/direct/system types, enforced by InvalidMessage validation on both build and parse.
Good separation of concerns — messages.py (schema), registry.py (concurrency), server.py (transport) — with the ClientRegistry guarding all mutation/iteration behind an asyncio.Lock.
Defensive broadcast: dead clients are detected via asyncio.gather(return_exceptions=True) and dropped from the registry, and system events (connected/joined/left) are broadcast on lifecycle changes.
Strong typing discipline throughout: full type hints, `from __future__ import annotations`, module docstrings, and exceptions wrapped with `from exc`.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-structured, spec-faithful greenfield session-1 implementation whose visible modules are convention-clean, but the full commit carries measurable naming debt (0.81 / 21 violations concentrated in app.py, store.py, transport.py, and __init__.py files not shown in the diff).

problems.description: New subscribe/unsubscribe protocol messages, two new HTTP endpoints (/channels, /channels/{name}/subscribers), and channel-scoped broadcast ship with no tests (+0 files, source-only diff).
broadcast_channel duplicates the target-selection-then-dead-client-drop logic already present in broadcast; the two could share a common send-and-drop helper.

Channel names accept any non-empty string with no charset restriction, yet are URL-decoded and matched by regex in the /channels/{name}/subscribers endpoint — loose validation on a surface that becomes path-like.

strengths: Extends the existing ClientRegistry pattern faithfully: broadcast_channel mirrors broadcast including dead-client drop semantics and reuses unregister, which correctly cleans up channel subscriptions.
Adds a _json_response static method that removes duplicated Content-Type header boilerplate across HTTP handlers.
Message-type dispatch follows the established if/elif chain, with system messages still correctly rejected from clients and subscribe/unsubscribe returning explicit acknowledgements.
Consistent snake_case methods, PascalCase classes, type hints, and docstrings; module-level compiled regex with urllib unquote for safe channel decoding.
Good lock discipline — registry mutations stay under the asyncio.Lock while I/O is hoisted outside it, matching existing patterns.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, pattern-following extension adding channel subscriptions to the notification server, consistent with the existing registry/broadcast design and improving HTTP response handling, though shipped without tests and with some duplicated broadcast logic. Note: the measured 0.81 convention score and listed violations come from files this commit never touched (app.py, __init__.py, store.py, transport.py) — the commit's own code adheres to codebase conventions.

problems.description: Redis-mirrored cluster state (CLIENTS_KEY / channel sets) is only reaped on graceful unregister; a crashed server instance leaves orphaned client/channel entries, so global_count() and exists() can report stale connections with no TTL/heartbeat or reaping mechanism.

subscribe() and register() await Redis round-trips while holding the asyncio.Lock, serializing local mutations behind network I/O; collecting state under the lock and issuing Redis calls after release would keep the hot path non-blocking.

Per static analysis, the commit's wider footprint (app.py, __init__.py, store.py, transport.py) accumulates 21 naming violations — module-level constants not UPPER_CASE, mixed snake_case/PascalCase for functions and classes — dragging the convention score to 0.81; these lie outside the shown redis_bus.py/registry.py diff, which itself conforms.

strengths: RedisBus is a clean asyncio pub/sub fan-out with proper cancellation, graceful teardown via contextlib.suppress, and malformed-message handling that drops and logs rather than crashing.
Backward-compatible extension: ClientRegistry preserves exact local-only behavior when redis_client is omitted, retaining the existing lock-based concurrency pattern.
Architectural intent is well documented in docstrings (envelope fan-out, every-instance-including-self delivery), and Redis keys use consistent namespacing with centralized _srem_channel cleanup.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid, well-documented Redis pub/sub integration that cleanly extends the existing registry with backward compatibility, offset by a 0.81 convention score (21 naming violations concentrated outside the shown diff) and a minor cluster-state staleness gap on instance crash.

problems.description: Rate limiting counts every inbound message (including rejected ones and non-content system traffic like subscribe/unsubscribe) against the same window; the docstring notes this is intentional, but it means a client past the limit stays rejected until the window rolls over with no grace path.
The /history HTTP endpoint is implemented inside the WebSocket transport's process_request seam; it works and reuses the existing seam, but couples transport and storage concerns slightly.

Measured convention score 0.81 is dragged down almost entirely by pre-existing seed-code violations in app.py, __init__.py and transport.py (untouched by this commit); the code this commit introduces (PascalCase RateLimiter, snake_case methods, UPPER_CASE DEFAULT_LIMIT/WINDOW_SECONDS/DEFAULT_MESSAGE_TTL_DAYS/CLEANUP_INTERVAL_SECONDS) adheres cleanly — flagging the discrepancy.

strengths: RateLimiter mirrors the established RedisBus/ClientRegistry optional-redis pattern exactly (shared cluster-wide counters with local in-memory fallback, key prefix consistent with existing notification_server:* keys).

Message expiry sweep is managed with the same lifecycle discipline as the bus listen task (cancel + contextlib.suppress(CancelledError) in close()), and blocking SQLite work is correctly offloaded via asyncio.to_thread like _persist.
store.py refactor extracts _row_to_dict and adds get_history with an efficient limit+1 has_more trick and a delete_older_than method — clean, well-documented, no redundant COUNT query.

Extensive test coverage added (test_rate_limiter, 272-line test_server, test_store, test_server_redis updates) with env-var-driven configuration consistent with the existing DATABASE_URL/REDIS_URL pattern.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-fitted cross-cutting session that adds cluster-wide rate limiting and message TTL expiry by faithfully reusing the codebase's optional-Redis dependency-injection pattern and task-lifecycle discipline, with the modest 0.81 convention score attributable to pre-existing seed-code violations rather than the new code.
